name: Zinc
lead: Zinc is an essential trace element in humans, a cofactor for many enzymes and the second most abundant trace metal in the body after iron [1][2]. For appearance it matters in three ways: as an oral supplement and nutrient involved in skin, hair and wound healing; as a topical ingredient, from zinc oxide in sunscreens, barrier creams and mineral makeup to zinc pyrithione in anti-dandruff shampoos; and as a mineral that looksmaxxing forums discuss alongside other supplements [3][25][26][27].

The chain people describe runs from adequate zinc status to calmer inflammatory acne, less shedding where hair loss is tied to deficiency, and better skin repair. A 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis found that people with acne had lower serum zinc than controls and that zinc treatment, as monotherapy or adjunct, was associated with a significant improvement in inflammatory papule counts, without a significant difference in side effects versus comparators [3]. Wikipedia describes acne, eczema, dry scaling skin, seborrheic dermatitis, impaired wound healing and thin, sparse hair among the signs of zinc deficiency [25].

Wikipedia states that deficiency affects roughly two billion people, mostly in the developing world, and that excess zinc may cause ataxia, lethargy and copper deficiency [1][25]. On looksmax.org zinc is discussed as a routine supplement, often next to peptides such as GHK-Cu, and in threads about forms, amounts and effects on the voice and libido [22][23][24].

paras: Zinc is used orally and topically for inflammatory acne, with proposed anti-inflammatory and antibacterial effects [3]. A 2024 review of zinc, copper and iron in selected skin diseases discusses the minerals' roles in skin conditions [8]. Zinc oxide is a skin-protectant ingredient; a US drug label for a zinc oxide diaper cream lists indications to help prevent and treat diaper rash and to protect chafed skin, with warnings for external use only and to avoid contact with eyes [7]. Hair shedding associated with zinc deficiency is described in clinical discussion of the mineral, with benefit generally expected when a deficiency exists [8][9].

Topically, zinc oxide absorbs both UVA and UVB light and is the broadest-spectrum UV absorber the US FDA approves for sunscreens; Wikipedia describes it as photostable and generally considered non-irritating and non-comedogenic, and many sunscreens use nanoparticle forms so that they do not leave a white cast [26]. It is also a main ingredient of mineral makeup, where it appears as CI 77947, and of baby powder, calamine lotion and barrier creams, and athletes use zinc oxide tape [26].

Zinc pyrithione, a zinc coordination compound first described in the 1930s, is the active ingredient in several anti-dandruff shampoos and body washes and is approved for over-the-counter use against dandruff and seborrhoeic dermatitis in the US; it inhibits fungal and bacterial growth [27]. The EU banned its use in cosmetic products from 2021 after classifying it as a category 1B reproductive toxicant, while US rules allow limited concentrations in rinse-off and leave-on products [27].

A 2024 systematic review of 38 randomised trials, commissioned by the WHO for revision of its guidelines, examined zinc for acute and persistent diarrhoea in children [10]. Zinc has also been studied for pneumonia in children, immune function, pressure ulcers, oral mucositis and other conditions [11][12][13][14].

Wikipedia lists acne, eczema, dry scaling skin, seborrheic dermatitis, delayed wound healing and alopecia with thin, sparse hair among the signs of zinc deficiency, together with delayed growth in children [25]. Causes include diets high in phytate-containing whole grains or low in zinc, gut diseases that impair absorption, heavy alcohol use, diarrhoea, chronic kidney or liver disease and bariatric surgery [25]. Mild deficiency from low dietary intake is described as common and severe deficiency as rare [25].

Plasma zinc is described as a limited biomarker; a blood level below about 70 mcg/dL is the usual threshold used with clinical suspicion [25]. Clinicians treat deficiency with oral zinc salts such as gluconate, sulfate or acetate, and the article notes it is unclear whether one form is better [25]. This is the setting in which proponents say zinc visibly changes skin and hair, since the repletion corrects the underlying shortfall.

Acrodermatitis enteropathica is an autosomal recessive disorder of zinc absorption caused by variants in the SLC39A4 gene, which encodes a zinc-uptake transporter [29]. It presents, often around weaning, with dermatitis around the body openings and on the fingers and toes, blistering, pustules, diarrhoea and hair loss that can include eyebrows and eyelashes; lifelong zinc supplementation is the treatment [29]. It is the textbook example of a skin and hair condition reversed by zinc [25][29].

Oral zinc has been studied in acne since at least 1978, when a controlled trial of zinc sulfate in acne vulgaris was published [15]. The 2020 meta-analysis reports lower serum zinc in acne patients and better inflammatory papule counts with zinc, and concludes that zinc has been used as monotherapy or adjunct [3]. A 2024 review of zinc, copper and iron in skin disease notes that most cited studies report lower serum zinc in acne patients, while findings on whether levels track severity conflict: some studies linked lower zinc to more severe acne and others found no link [8].

Proposed mechanisms are anti-inflammatory and antibacterial actions and effects on keratinocyte function [3][4]. Researchers also note that zinc status is discussed alongside copper and iron in other skin diseases such as atopic dermatitis and psoriasis, where results on serum levels are inconsistent [8].

Acne: the 2020 meta-analysis reported significantly lower serum zinc in acne patients and an improvement in inflammatory papule counts with zinc treatment, with no significant difference in side-effect incidence [3]. An early controlled trial of zinc sulfate in acne vulgaris was published in 1978 [15].

Other areas: a Cochrane review of nutritional interventions for pressure ulcers (2024) is among the wound-related syntheses [12]; a randomised trial tested zinc chloride mouthwash for chemotherapy-related oral mucositis [13]; and a 2025 randomised trial tested zinc as adjuvant treatment in SARS-CoV-2 [16]. A 2024 crossover trial reported improved absorption of a glycoprotein matrix zinc form [17]. Registered trials include absorption studies of zinc citrate, gluconate and oxide, childhood pneumonia (641 participants) and a large 2026 trial of zinc and infections in older medical patients [18][19][20]. A 2017 review describes zinc as a gatekeeper of immune function [21].

Wikipedia notes that consumption of excess zinc may cause ataxia and lethargy, among other effects [1]. Grokipedia describes zinc as non-toxic at typical dietary levels and notes that inhaling zinc oxide dust can cause metal fume fever [2]. The 2020 acne meta-analysis found no significant difference in side-effect incidence between zinc and comparators [3].

Wikipedia's article on zinc toxicity reports that very high oral intakes can cause nausea, vomiting, cramps and diarrhoea, that long-term high intake has been linked to changes in blood lipids, and that reduced copper levels and zinc-induced sideroblastic anaemia have been described in the literature; the copper changes reversed when zinc intake stopped [28]. Inhaling zinc oxide fumes, for example when welding galvanised steel, can cause metal fume fever [28]. Excess zinc absorption suppressing copper absorption is the reason zinc and copper are often discussed together on forums [1][24][28].

Dietary zinc comes from oysters, red meat, nuts and fortified cereals, per Grokipedia, which gives adult recommended intakes of 11 mg per day for men and 8 mg for women [2]. Wikipedia notes that diets built around high-phytate whole grains, or foods grown in zinc-poor soil, are common causes of low intake [25]. Supplements are sold as sulfate, gluconate, acetate, citrate and oxide salts and as chelated or matrix forms, and registered and published bioavailability trials have compared several of them [5][6][17]. Wikipedia says it is unclear whether any one supplement form is better for treating deficiency [25].

Reviews describe zinc as a cofactor for many enzymes with roles in immune regulation and wound healing, and the acne, wound-healing and dermatitis research builds on those roles [4][21]. Wikipedia adds that zinc is the only metal found in all enzyme classes and is required for prenatal and postnatal development [1].

Zinc is the only metal found in all enzyme classes, is required for prenatal and postnatal development, and deficiency in children is linked to growth retardation, delayed sexual maturation, infection susceptibility and diarrhoea [1]. A 2024 review covers its role in health and disease, including immune regulation and wound healing [9][21]. Absorption differs between forms, which has been compared in small bioavailability trials [17][18].

Zinc ores were used to make brass long before the metal was identified; metallic zinc was produced in India, with distillation evidence at the Zawar mines by the 9th century and the name zincum credited to Paracelsus in the 16th century; Andreas Marggraf is credited with isolating pure zinc in 1746 [1]. Zinc was found in the enzyme carbonic anhydrase in 1940, which showed its biological role, and carboxypeptidase followed in 1955 [1].

Zinc's nutritional status developed in the 20th century: it was found essential for rat growth in 1933 and shown to be essential for human growth in 1963, the first case of acrodermatitis enteropathica was described in 1973, and in 1974 the US National Academy of Sciences declared it essential and set a recommended allowance [25]. The FDA required zinc in total parenteral nutrition fluids from 1978, and the gut zinc transporter ZIP4 was identified in 2002 [25]. In dermatology, zinc sulfate was trialled for acne in 1978 [15], while zinc oxide has an older history as a salve and later as a white pigment and sunscreen ingredient [26].

Zinc is a widely sold dietary supplement, with gluconate, sulfate, acetate, citrate and oxide forms on the market, and bioavailability of different forms has been compared in small trials [5][6][17]. Zinc oxide is regulated in the US as a sunscreen active and skin-protectant ingredient, and is on the FDA's generally-recognised-as-safe list for food use [7][26].

In looksmaxxing communities zinc appears in threads about acne, immunity, and hormonal or voice effects, usually as one item in a supplement stack, and in Turkish-language threads about whether zinc affects erections [30]. Forum members ask which form is best, how long to take it and whether copper should be supplemented afterwards, and answers are anecdotal [22][24].

timeline.event: Distillation of nearly pure zinc is evidenced at the Zawar mines in Rajasthan, India [1].
Andreas Marggraf is credited with isolating pure metallic zinc [1].
Zinc is found in carbonic anhydrase, showing its biological importance [1].
Zinc is shown to be essential for human growth [25].
First case of acrodermatitis enteropathica described [25].
US National Academy of Sciences declares zinc essential and sets an allowance [25].
Controlled trial of zinc sulfate in acne vulgaris is published [15].
ZIP4 identified as the gut zinc absorption mechanism [25].
Meta-analysis reports lower serum zinc in acne and improved inflammatory papule counts with zinc [3].
EU bans zinc pyrithione in cosmetic products [27].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org zinc is discussed as a routine supplement, often taken with peptides such as GHK-Cu, with threads on amounts, forms, voice effects, libido and what to do after taking too much [22][23][24].

claims.claim: Zinc should be supplemented at around 30 to 50 mg per day while using GHK-Cu.
claims.believers: In a looksmax.org thread on zinc and GHK-Cu, one user asked whether zinc was needed during a month of GHK-Cu and replies said yes, with one user saying he takes 30 mg daily and another asking about 50 mg [22].
claims.experts: No published studies of zinc dosing alongside GHK-Cu exist. Wikipedia notes that consumption of excess zinc may cause ataxia and lethargy [1].

claims.claim: Zinc made a user's voice deeper.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread titled 'zinc made my voice deeper' presents this as a personal report [23].
claims.experts: Wikipedia links zinc deficiency in children to delayed sexual maturation [1]. No published studies of zinc supplementation and voice pitch have been identified.

claims.claim: Excess zinc intake requires copper supplementation afterwards.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread titled 'should i supplement copper after zinc overdose' asks whether copper should be taken after taking too much zinc [24].
claims.experts: A 2024 review discusses zinc, copper and iron together in skin disease [8], and Wikipedia lists ataxia, lethargy and copper deficiency among effects of excess zinc, with excess zinc absorption able to suppress copper absorption [1][28].

claims.believers: Forum members and supplement users say zinc calms breakouts, and Turkish-language posters mention starting it for both immunity and acne [30].
claims.experts: A 2020 meta-analysis found lower serum zinc in acne patients and improved inflammatory papule counts with zinc treatment [3]; a 2024 review reports conflicting results on whether zinc levels track acne severity [8].

claims.believers: Supplement users describe zinc as a hair and skin mineral.
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists alopecia among the signs of zinc deficiency and describes acrodermatitis enteropathica, in which hair loss resolves with lifelong zinc supplementation [25][29]. Benefit is generally described where a deficiency exists [8][9].

claims.believers: A Turkish-language looksmax.org thread relays a claim that someone's erections stopped because of zinc, and other members reply that it is a common mineral and not a drug [30].
claims.experts: Wikipedia links childhood zinc deficiency to delayed sexual maturation [1]. No published trials of zinc supplementation and erectile function in zinc-replete men have been identified.

claims.claim: Zinc oxide sunscreens protect skin from ageing and burns.
claims.believers: Mineral-sunscreen users prefer zinc oxide as a broad-spectrum, non-irritating filter.
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports zinc oxide is an FDA-approved UVA and UVB sunscreen ingredient and that nanoparticles remain in the outermost skin layer [26].

chain: Adequate zinc status, orally or via topical zinc products
Support for skin repair, sebum and inflammation control, and hair growth where deficiency exists
Calmer acne, less deficiency-related shedding, and protected or sun-shielded skin
angle.text: People take zinc for inflammatory acne and for hair shedding associated with low zinc, and apply zinc oxide as a sunscreen filter, barrier cream or mineral-makeup base. Zinc pyrithione shampoos are used to keep dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis in check.
